expectations.text: Identifies AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE as an AWS access key finding and states it is present in both the current working tree and git history
expectations.evidence: '[HIGH] AWS credential pair, still in working tree AND history ... Present in: current working tree (HEAD) and every commit since 973222e'.

expectations.text: Identifies the RSA private key block as a finding present ONLY in git history — explicitly notes it was removed from the current working tree in a later commit
expectations.evidence: '[HIGH] RSA private key block, git history only ... **Not present in current working tree**', naming both the introducing and removing commits.

expectations.text: Masks both secret values in the report, e.g. showing only a few leading/trailing characters (such as AKIA****MPLE) rather than the full key or full private key body
expectations.evidence: Findings carry 'Masked: AKIA****MPLE / wJal****EKEY' and 'Masked: MIIF****AAAA'.

expectations.text: Remediation for both findings explicitly says to rotate the credential (not merely delete, purge, or gitignore it)
expectations.evidence: 'Both findings are in committed history, so per policy: **rotate, don't just remove.** Rotate/revoke the AWS key pair with AWS IAM ... Treat the private key as compromised and reissue it'.

expectations.text: Recommends git filter-repo (or BFG Repo-Cleaner) for purging the history, and does not recommend git rebase -i or git commit --amend as a history-rewriting strategy
expectations.evidence: 'git filter-repo --path config/credentials.txt --invert-paths (not rebase -i/commit --amend — those leave reflog traces)'.

expectations.text: The response never prints the full RSA private key body or the full AWS secret access key value anywhere, even while explaining the finding
expectations.evidence: VIOLATION: after masking the finding, the prose prints both full literal values — AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE and wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY — while arguing they are AWS's documented placeholders.
